name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
title: Funder Formatting and Compliance
answer: Funder formatting and compliance covers the mechanical and administrative requirements that a grant proposal must meet before a funding body will review it. This includes page limits, font and margin rules, required sections such as data management and broader impacts, budget forms, and certification of institutional approvals. For AI research proposals it also extends to statements on compute resources, model release, data provenance, and reproducibility. The topic sits inside grant proposals and funding because formatting errors or missing compliance elements can remove an otherwise strong proposal from consideration.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard document preparation and submission systems rather than specialised AI infrastructure. Researchers typically prepare proposals in word processors or LaTeX, convert them to PDF, and upload them through funder portals that validate file type, page count, and section presence. Institutional systems hold boilerplate text, budget templates, and approval workflows. Reference managers and shared drives support the assembly of citations, biosketches, and letters of support.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by reading the solicitation line by line and extracting every binding requirement into a checklist. The proposal is then drafted to fit those constraints, with repeated passes to trim text, adjust figures, and confirm that each required element appears under the correct heading. A second reader checks the final PDF against the funder's published rules before submission. For AI proposals, this also means checking that data and code availability statements match what the project will actually produce.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on whether a proposal is accepted for review at all, since noncompliance can lead to administrative rejection without scientific evaluation. Funder rules also create ongoing obligations after an award, such as open access publication, data sharing, and reporting on model or dataset use. Provenance matters because applicants must show where data, code, and prior results come from, and must not claim rights they do not hold. Institutions manage these risks through pre-submission review and by keeping records of approvals and certifications.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Funder formatting and compliance is moving toward structured, machine-readable application data that can be checked automatically before human review. Funders are increasingly asking for persistent identifiers, FAIR data plans, and explicit statements on compute and environmental cost. Compliance checks are likely to become more integrated into drafting tools, flagging missing sections or overlong text as the proposal is written. The direction is toward less manual page counting and more continuous verification against a funder's published rules.
